title: CFA Ethics 30: Standard IV(A) - how to leave a job properly
subtitle: Before you go, after you go, and the limits of inviting clients to follow
whyItMatters: Everyone changes jobs, and this is the one standard where an ordinary career decision turns into a breach purely because of sequence - doing it after you leave is fine, doing it before you leave is not.
openingQuestion: You are about to resign and set up your own firm. During your last month in the job, what may you do?
openingOptions: Prepare everything, including approaching your current clients in advance
Handle the administrative preparation, but without using the firm's resources
Nothing at all until the day the resignation formally takes effect
Whatever you like, as long as your current output does not suffer
explanation: Standard IV(A) does not prohibit preparing to leave - that would be absurd. It prohibits using your current employer's resources to compete with them while still drawing their salary. The line falls on specific conduct: renting an office and registering a company are fine, because that is administrative preparation. Approaching clients to invite them across, copying the client list, or taking the firm's valuation model with you are not, because all three take the employer's property and use it against them. Once you have left, approaching former clients using publicly available information is legitimate - unless a separate non-compete agreement binds you.

summary.keyIdea: The line is not whether you intend to leave but whose resources you are spending to prepare for it.
summary.commonMistake: Soliciting clients while still employed. After you leave, using public information, it is permitted; before you leave, it is not.

application.title: The practical boundary
application.message: Anything created with the firm's time and resources belongs to the firm - including a model you built out of hours on their machine.

sections.text: Standard IV(A) does not prohibit preparing to leave - that would be absurd. It prohibits using your current employer's resources to compete with them while still drawing their salary.

left.label: Before leaving - permitted
left.text: Renting an office, registering a company, talking to a prospective employer, handling administrative formalities out of hours.

right.label: Before leaving - not permitted
right.text: Approaching clients to invite them across, copying the client list, taking the firm's valuation model with you.

sections.text: The three prohibited acts share one feature: they take the employer's property - client relationships, data, intellectual output - and use it against the employer.

sections.label: The cleanest way to tell them apart
sections.text: The knowledge in your head travels with you. The files on the machine belong to the firm. The fact that you also happen to remember what is in those files does not make copying them legitimate.

The Standard IV(A) duty ends. Approaching former clients using publicly available information is legitimate - unless a separate non-compete agreement binds you, and that agreement is a matter of contract rather than of the professional standards.

One further situation falls under this standard: taking a second job. It needs the employer's prior consent, even where the work is in an unrelated field, because they are the only party able to judge whether it creates a conflict or takes time that was owed to them.

lines: You have the right to leave.
You do not have the right to take what is not yours.

diagram.label: Before leaving: administrative preparation is fine
Before leaving: soliciting clients and copying data are not
After leaving: contact using public information is fine
Unless a separate non-compete agreement applies

realWorldExample.company: Knowledge in your head and files on the machine
realWorldExample.description: The practical line courts and disciplinary bodies tend to use: the professional skill and knowledge you have accumulated belong to you and travel with you. Documents, models, client lists and data created by the firm belong to the firm, even where you built them with your own hands on company time. This is why an analyst can rebuild a similar valuation model at a new firm - using their own knowledge - but may not carry the old file across.

quiz.question: What does Standard IV(A) prohibit while you are still employed?
options: Talking to any other employer about a new job opportunity at all
Every form of preparation for whatever your next role turns out to be
Using the firm's resources to compete with that very firm
Taking part in professional activities outside your working hours
quiz.explanation: Prohibiting preparation to leave would be absurd, since nobody could ever move jobs. What is prohibited is taking property belonging to the party paying you and turning it against them. Talking to prospective employers, preparing administratively and attending professional events out of hours all leave the employer's property untouched.

quiz.question: Which of these is permitted before you formally resign?
options: Taking a copy of a valuation model you built with your own hands
Approaching clients in advance to invite them to follow you across
Copying the client list to use at the place you are moving to
Renting an office and registering the new company you are forming
quiz.explanation: Administrative preparation touches neither the employer's property nor its clients, so it sits outside the prohibition. The other three all take something the firm owns. Having built the model yourself does not change its ownership: work created on company time and resources belongs to the company, however much of it came out of your own head.

quiz.question: Once you have left, may you contact former clients?
options: Yes, if you use public information and no agreement forbids it
Never, because those clients belong to your previous employer
Only once the previous employer has given written consent to it
Only with clients who approached you first of their own accord
quiz.explanation: The duty of loyalty ends when the employment relationship does; what remains afterwards is whatever separate agreements were signed. Clients are not owned by anyone, so a permanent prohibition has no basis, and requiring the former employer's consent would hand a competitor a veto the standard never gave them.

quiz.question: Who owns a valuation model you built during working hours?
options: You, because it is the intellectual output of your own mind
The firm, even though you built it with your own hands
Both parties jointly, in proportion to their contributions
The clients who paid fees for analysis produced using it
quiz.explanation: The knowledge needed to rebuild the model belongs to you; the specific file does not. This is the most widely used practical boundary, and it is what lets a departing analyst rebuild something similar at the new firm without carrying anything across. Joint ownership and client ownership are not how employment or professional work product operate.

quiz.question: What about taking a second job while still employed full time?
options: It is entirely prohibited under Standard IV(A) as it stands
It is freely permitted as long as it falls outside office hours
You must disclose it and obtain the employer's consent first
You need only disclose it if it is in the same financial field
quiz.explanation: This is where Standard IV(A) meets IV(B): the employer is the party who assesses the conflict, so they have to be told in order to assess it. An outright prohibition would go further than the standard does, and both the 'outside hours' and 'same field' tests substitute your own judgement for the assessment that belongs to them.

keyTakeaways: Preparing to leave is not prohibited - using the firm's resources to compete with it is
Before leaving: renting an office is fine, soliciting clients and copying data are not
After leaving: contact using public information is fine, absent a separate agreement
Knowledge in your head travels with you; files on the machine belong to the firm
A second job needs the employer's prior consent

practicePrompt.question: On your last working day, you email the client list announcing your move to a new firm and giving your contact details. Assessment?
options: Legitimate, since this is your final working day at the firm
A breach: the client list is the property of the firm
Legitimate if the email only announces and does not solicit business
A breach only if some clients actually move across with you
practicePrompt.explanation: Two separate problems at once, and either alone would be enough. The last day is still a day inside the employment relationship. And using the client list - the firm's property - for your own purposes is a breach whatever the email says. The final option fails for a familiar reason: if only consequences counted, every unsuccessful attempt would go free.
